title: Comments of the Alaska Public Interest Research Group on the Preliminary Permit Application for the DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute and Infrastructure Hub Project under P-15423.

documents.name: 2610_ENE_FERC-Cook-Inlet_Comment.docx.pdf
documents.text:
October 21, 2026

To: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

From: Alaska Public Interest Research Group

RE: Docket Number P-15423, DeepGreen Cook Inlet Application for Preliminary Permit

The Alaska Public Interest Research Group (AKPIRG) submits the following comments on the
preliminary permit application for the DeepGreen Cook Inlet project. AKPIRG is a statewide,
nonpartisan 501(c)(3) nonprofit with over 50 years of history advocating for the public interest in
Alaska. We work to empower Alaskans, strengthen transparent and accountable government,
and advance policies that best serve the public.

On February 11, 2026, DeepGreen Cook Inlet SVP LLC, a Delaware-based company created
this year, filed a preliminary permit application with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
(FERC). In June, FERC informed DeepGreen that their application had several deficiencies: the
failure to include all possible Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations that may be affected by the
project; the lack of dimensions and physical composition information for the proposed
structures; and the failure to include the mailing address for the City of Kenai in the application.1
DeepGreen filed a response to FERC just over a week later, remedying the deficiencies outlined
by FERC. The project detailed in the application would be a 100-megawatt tidal energy high
performance computing facility. The project would include up to 350 turbines that would be
simultaneously powered and cooled by the tides and water of Cook Inlet.2 The project plans
include connecting to Alaska Energy Authority’s Cook Inlet PowerLink (CIPLink), which is still in
the funding stage of the development process with a targeted completion date of 2032.3 The
proposed project presents several concerns and challenges, including the lack of engagement
with potential stakeholders and the public as a whole, and the Applicant’s indication that they
would like to explore strategic partnerships with regional Alaska Native Corporations and local
entities, without including more information and details as to what those partnerships would
entail.

 As a public interest advocacy organization, AKPIRG’s predominant concern with DeepGreen’s
application is the lack of communication and coordination with those that would be most directly
impacted by this proposal. As FERC noted in their notification of application deficiencies to
DeepGreen, the Applicant failed to include any Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations that may
be affected by the proposed project. In their original application, DeepGreen identified only one
Tribe that could be affected. In FERC’s response, FERC outlines six Tribal organizations that
should have been included in the application. We appreciate that DeepGreen outlines these
additional organizations that they have updated to include in their application, but the lack of
inclusion in the initial filing demonstrates that DeepGreen has insufficient knowledge and
understanding of local Tribal organizations and Alaska Native Corporations. This raises
concerns for how the Applicant will appropriately and adequately engage with those most
affected by this project. DeepGreen has proposed a similar project in Eastport, Maine on the
Bay of Fundy, an area known, like Cook Inlet, for its strong tides. In this application as well,
FERC responded with a notice of deficiency highlighting several Tribes that DeepGreen failed to
identify and list in their application. The City of Eastport has engaged with FERC as an
intervener, with the City Council specifically requesting that DeepGreen does more early
engagement and consultation with the City and Tribal governments and communities. This
furthermore highlights the Applicant’s history of shortcomings when it comes to proactively
engaging with community members affected by their projects.

Additionally, as highlighted by FERC in the notification of application deficiencies, DeepGreen
did not include the City of Kenai’s contact information in their initial filing, as required by FERC
guidelines. In their initial statement, DeepGreen lists the location of the proposal as being within
the Kenai Peninsula Borough. However, based on the Motion to Intervene filed by the Kenai
Peninsula Borough on September 11, there has been a lack of engagement between
DeepGreen and the Borough.4 While the Kenai Peninsula Borough is clear in their motion that
they are not yet taking a position on the project, they are filing to be included in the notice
requirements for future filings related to DeepGreen’s application. It is concerning that they were
not included in DeepGreen’s previous communications.

Furthermore, DeepGreen’s application details plans to connect the project to the CIPLink
project, a high-voltage 38-mile subsea cable from the Kenai Peninsula to the Anchorage and
MatSu regions under the purview of the Alaska Energy Authority (AEA). However, Curtis Thayer,
CEO of the Alaska Energy Authority, has stated that he found out about the project from the
FERC filing and that DeepGreen had not previously reached out to AEA.5 This further raises
concerns both about DeepGreen’s commitment to working with stakeholders along with the
technological viability of their proposed project - given they have not worked with AEA to best
understand how their project would integrate with AEA’s CIPLink project. Additionally, as

 mentioned previously, CIPLink is still in the proposal stage and is estimated to take eight years
to complete - raising questions of the true feasibility of DeepGreen’s plan to connect to CIPLink.

Beyond the lack of engagement at this time, we also have concerns about DeepGreen’s plan to
explore “strategic partnerships with regional Native Corporations and local entities.”6 Our
concerns are not with these potential partnerships as a whole, as we encourage DeepGreen to
proactively engage with local organizations, but rather with the nature of what the partnerships
would entail. In Alaska, there is a long history of extractive industries coming into rural and
remote communities throughout the State. In this case, if DeepGreen does want to explore
strategic partnerships, we advocate for the use of legally binding agreements to ensure
developers hold their word in these partnerships. Community benefits agreements are growing
in use throughout the country because they allow communities to negotiate with developers and
execute legally binding contracts to protect community needs and interests. We specifically ask
that the Applicant be more detailed and transparent in their future application materials as to
what these strategic partnerships would entail.

To summarize, AKPIRG’s main concerns are with the initial lack of engagement, coordination,
and outreach on DeepGreen’s behalf with stakeholders and the general public as a whole. We
want to emphasize the importance of developers, especially those that are new to the state,
appropriately, adequately, and proactively engaging with local Tribal organizations, Alaska
Native Corporations, and local governments. This project’s application raises more questions
than answers, and we encourage DeepGreen to review their processes for both stakeholder
and public engagement in the future. We also encourage both FERC and DeepGreen to review
the numerous comments submitted by concerned members of the public, which highlight a wide
range of issues with this proposal.

We appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments and thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,




Gratia Rowell, AKPIRG Energy Policy Analyst




June Okada, AKPIRG Energy Director
